source: Wilhelm, Diekelmann, Molzow, Ayoub, Moelle, Born (2011) Sleep selectively enhances memory expected to be of future relevance (Exp 1, word pairs)
finding: Sleep helped word-pair recall only when people were told of the later test. Without that information sleep gave no gain over wake. Wake groups were not affected by expectancy.
numbers: Exp 1 N=142 (104 in the main analysis). Retention after sleep: expected 117.29 +/- 3.54% vs unexpected 105.23 +/- 3.01% (p=0.014). Wake groups 96.7 to 104.9% (expected) and 99.1 to 101.3% (unexpected). Expectancy x sleep/wake interaction p=0.05. Stage 4 sleep 8.2% vs 4.07% (p=0.03).
quote: Sleep preferentially benefits consolidation of memories that are relevant for future behavior
limits: Interaction was only borderline (p=0.05). Subjects who suspected the test were dropped from the unexpected group, a flexible exclusion. Small cells (about 18 per sleep group in the physiology analysis). Single lab.
agent_relevance: Founding result for 'future relevance decides what sleep keeps'. Treat it as a hypothesis with weak-to-moderate support, not a law, when designing a keep/drop rule.

source: Wilhelm, Diekelmann, Molzow, Ayoub, Moelle, Born (2011) Sleep selectively enhances memory expected to be of future relevance (Exp 2, locations and finger tapping)
finding: Expectancy also raised overnight retention of card locations and finger sequence tapping, and raised slow oscillation activity. Slow oscillation power and spindle count correlated with retention only in the expecting group.
numbers: Exp 2 N=49. Card locations: expected 98.80 +/- 4.92% vs unexpected 73.13 +/- 9.08% (p=0.019). Exp 1 correlation of first-20-min slow oscillation power with retention r=0.71 in expected group vs r=-0.25 in unexpected. Suspecting subjects: 89.67% (p=0.17 vs unexpected, not significant).
limits: Exp 2 had no wake control, so it cannot show the effect is sleep-specific. Correlations rest on n of about 18-21 per cell and are likely inflated (winner's curse).
agent_relevance: Mechanism sketch: an expected-use flag at learning leads to more consolidation work later. Our analogue is a will-be-needed flag set at write time.

source: Van Dongen, Thielen, Takashima, Barth, Fernandez (2012) Sleep supports selective retention of associative memories based on relevance for future utilization
finding: After learning two sets of picture-location pairs, people were told only one set would be retested. After a night of sleep the relevant set was kept better. After a day awake the relevant set was kept worse than the irrelevant set.
numbers: N=60 tested, 50 analysed (10 excluded for doubting the instruction). 3-way interaction F=13.19, p=0.001. Sleep: relevant loss -1.8 vs irrelevant -3.1 (diff 1.3 +/- 0.6, p=0.045). Wake: relevant -5.0 vs irrelevant -3.3 (diff -1.7, p=0.005). Sleep vs wake on relevant items diff 3.2 +/- 1.0, p=0.003; on irrelevant items p=0.83. 15 of 25 sleepers favoured relevant items.
quote: participants who slept longer forgot fewer associations from the relevant category
limits: Effect inside the sleep group alone is p=0.045. Participants were paid by performance at retest (reward confound). 17% of participants excluded. Not repeated in a similar sleep-only design (see Davidson review).
agent_relevance: Clean within-person design: same store, two tags, only one tag survives. Good template for testing a keep/drop rule in our agent.

source: Reverberi et al (2020) No evidence for an effect of explicit relevance instruction on consolidation of associative memories (as reported in Davidson and Pace-Schott 2021 review, Table 10)
finding: A close repeat of the Van Dongen design with a sleep-only group found no difference between relevant and irrelevant items. No sleep variable correlated with memory.
numbers: N=38, overnight sleep, within-subject relevance (all expecting a test for half the items). Reported as no main effect of expectancy. Actigraphy correlations: none.
limits: Known only through the review table; the original paper (Neuropsychologia 2020) was not opened. No wake control, so it cannot test the interaction.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of the closest relevance-instruction design. Lowers confidence that instruction-based tags are strong.

source: Wamsley, Hamilton, Graveline, Manceor, Parr (2016) Test Expectation Enhances Memory Consolidation across Both Sleep and Wake
finding: Telling people a test is coming improved memory for a virtual maze and a motor sequence task, but equally after sleep and after wake. The key sleep x expectation interaction was null.
numbers: N=100 (74 Furman, 26 Boston College). Maze completion time: expectation F(1,71)=7.35, p=.008, partial eta2=0.09; sleep x expectation F=0.77, p=.38. Distance F=0.55, p=.46. Backtracking F=0.0003, p=.99. Motor: expectation F(1,89)=4.18, p=.04; interaction F=0.96, p=.33. 70% of the unexpected-test subjects said they suspected a test.
quote: fail to support the hypothesis that the 'future relevance' of learned material moderates its consolidation selectively during sleep
limits: Procedural and spatial tasks, not word pairs. Suspicion in 70% of the unexpected group blurs the contrast. Reclassifying by suspicion still gave expectation effects.
agent_relevance: Relevance can raise retention by routes that do not need sleep (attention, rehearsal). A relevance tag may help for reasons unrelated to an offline step, so do not assume a delay or replay stage is what makes it work.

source: Stamm, Nguyen, Seicol, Fagan, Oh, Drumm, Lundt, Stickgold, Wamsley (2014) Negative reinforcement impairs overnight memory consolidation
finding: Adding a ticking monetary reward to a maze task made overnight improvement worse, not better. The authors suggest a stress route.
numbers: Sleep-only design, N=65 (per Davidson review Table 12). Reward effect was reversed on 2 of 4 outcomes. No wake group.
limits: Reward was a countdown (negative reinforcement), not a promised bonus. Only the abstract was read in the paper itself; the N and outcome count come from the review table.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: pressure framing can harm retention. A must-remember flag in a prompt may not help if it reads as a threat.

source: Davidson, Pace-Schott (2021) Does Sleep Selectively Strengthen Certain Memories Over Others Based on Emotion and Perceived Future Relevance?
finding: Systematic review of studies on emotion, reward, test expectancy, subjective relevance and forgetting instructions. Most studies do not show sleep-selective effects. No sleep variable reliably predicts which memory is picked.
numbers: No meta-analysis possible. Test expectancy: 4 papers (Wilhelm 2011, Van Dongen 2012, Wamsley 2016, Reverberi 2020); sleep x expectancy interaction in 2 of 4. Authors say effects are probably much smaller than often suggested.
quote: the majority of studies does not support such an effect
limits: Narrative review, no pooled effect. Underpowered studies (one participant per night in a lab) are named as the main cause of mixed findings.
agent_relevance: Best single summary of what holds up: the claim that sleep keeps what is relevant is a minority-result claim. Do not build the schema on it as an established fact.

source: Davidson, Pace-Schott (2021) review, reward studies table
finding: Reward and sleep: some positive (Fischer and Born 2009 N=76; Tamaki 2020 N=47 and N=40; Prehn-Kristensen 2018 children N=16), some null (Tucker 2011 N=75 and N=77; Oudiette 2013 N=30; Lo 2016; Prehn-Kristensen adults N=20; Baran 2013 N=38).
numbers: Of 12 datasets with a sleep x reward test in Table 12, the interaction was reported in 4 (Fischer and Born, Prehn-Kristensen children, Tamaki x2), mixed in 2 (Igloi 2015 at 3 months only; Sopp 2021 recognition only) and absent in 6 (my count). Oudiette 2013 without cueing: high-reward items better remembered in sleep and wake alike.
limits: Counts are my reading of one table. Reward types differ across studies (promised bonus, water drops, countdown).
agent_relevance: Value tags (reward) do raise retention in many designs, often regardless of sleep. A value-based or usage-based keep score is plausible, but the offline step is not shown to be the cause.

source: Davidson, Pace-Schott (2021) review, directed forgetting and retrieval-induced forgetting tables
finding: Forgetting instructions: Saletin 2011 found a nap boosted remember items only; Scullin 2017 partly repeated this in young adults for free recall but not recognition and not in older adults; Rauchs 2011 did not. List-method: Abel and Baeuml 2013 found less instruction effect after sleep; Hupbach 2018 and Blaskovich 2017 found no interaction.
numbers: Item-method: Saletin N=46 positive, Scullin N=50 young partly positive and N=45 older null, Rauchs N=25 null. List-method: Abel and Baeuml two datasets (N=128, N=112) positive, Blaskovich N=112 and Hupbach N=92 null.
limits: Designs differ (nap vs night, deprivation vs daytime wake). Retrieval-induced forgetting is also mixed: Abel and Baeuml 2012 found it only in sleepers, Baran 2010 found a larger effect in wake.
agent_relevance: Drop-by-instruction gives an inconsistent forgetting effect. In our agent, dropping should be an explicit deletion or demotion, not a tag we hope will make a trace fade.

source: Saletin, Goldstein, Walker (2011) The role of sleep in directed forgetting and remembering of human memories
finding: A nap kept words cued remember better than a no-nap control, but did not raise recall of words cued forget. The size of the remember-minus-forget gap tracked fast spindles over left parietal cortex.
numbers: N=46 (23 nap, 23 no-nap). Group x cue-type interaction F(2,43)=6.17, p=0.004. Group main effect F(1,44)=6.44, p=0.015. Remember-minus-forget efficiency t(44)=2.18, p=0.03. Fast spindle link at P3 survived multiple-comparison correction.
quote: sleep did not ubiquitously facilitate all items
limits: Free recall of forget words may sit near floor. p=0.03 for the key contrast. Later partial failures to repeat (Scullin 2017 older adults, Rauchs 2011).
agent_relevance: Closest human match to a keep list and a drop list: keep items gain, drop items are not helped. The drop list is left alone, not actively erased.

source: Feld, Born (2020) Neurochemical mechanisms for memory processing during sleep (Neuropsychopharmacology)
finding: The review states two accounts of how sleep picks high-reward memories: dopamine acts during sleep replay, or a tag set at learning raises replay frequency with no dopamine needed in sleep. It concludes selectivity most likely comes from up- or down-regulated reactivation frequency.
numbers: Pramipexole (D2 agonist) before sleep wiped out the high-over-low reward advantage while the encoding-strength advantage stayed. Sulpiride (about 60% D2 block) did not change the reward advantage. Weakly encoded memories are replayed more, so replay frequency is not just memory strength.
quote: highly relevant memories may be tagged by a dopaminergic process during learning that simply enhances replay of these memories during sleep
limits: Review. It admits rewards give less consistent effects, cites negative reinforcement impairing consolidation (Stamm 2014) and no effect over first-half slow-wave sleep (Tucker 2011), and says the D1 route is not excluded.
agent_relevance: The reconciliation: a tag at encoding sets the replay quota, and sleep does the work. For us the cheap computable tag is set at write time (expected future use); replay frequency is a quota, not a switch.

source: Feld, Born (2020) review: erasing irrelevant memories and synaptic downscaling
finding: The authors write that sleep may also serve to erase irrelevant memories and may restore hippocampal encoding capacity once systems consolidation makes traces redundant. NonREM strengthens cortical synapses while NonREM plus REM downregulate hippocampal ones.
numbers: No new data. Claim rests on refs 57, 59, 70-73 and on Wilhelm 2011 (ref 62).
limits: Hedged wording (may, likely). The authors note it is unclear what factors set the direction of plasticity.
agent_relevance: Supports a two-part rule for our store: strengthen what is expected to be needed, and free capacity from traces made redundant. The rule that sets direction is an open question.

source: Lipinska, Stuart, Thomas, Baldwin, Bolinger (2019) Preferential Consolidation of Emotional Memory During Sleep: A Meta-Analysis
finding: Pooled test of whether sleep favours emotional over neutral material. No overall effect. Stronger effects appeared with free recall, with controls for initial learning, and with full-night designs.
numbers: 31 studies, 36 datasets, random effects. No overall effect for negative, positive or combined versus neutral. Moderators: free recall over recognition; controlling initial learning; full night plus daytime wake control over nap plus deprivation.
limits: Treats emotional and neutral scores as independent (criticised by Schaefer et al, per Davidson review). Schaefer reportedly found REM-rich sleep helped emotional items but no recognition effect overall.
agent_relevance: Emotion is a rival relevance cue and the pooled test does not support strong sleep-specific prioritisation. Warns against treating salience as the keep signal.

source: Stickgold, Walker (2013) Sleep-dependent memory triage (listed on Europe PMC; full text fetch failed with HTTP 500)
finding: Review proposing that sleep triages memories by salience and relevance. Not opened this session.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not read; cited as part of the triage framework in other papers.
agent_relevance: Background only. Do not cite figures from it.

source: Huelin Gorriz, Takigawa, Bendor (2023) The role of experience in prioritizing hippocampal replay (Nature Communications)
finding: In rats, sleep replay rate rose with the number of laps run and fell with familiarity of a track. Awake replay counts during the task predicted what got sleep replay.
numbers: 19 sessions from 4 male rats, two tracks per session. Sleep replay track 1 vs track 2: p=0.0002 (POST1) and p=0.002 (later POST), two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank. Replay bias scaled with lap count.
limits: 4 animals; spatial memory only; the link between awake and sleep replay is correlational. Does not test task relevance directly.
agent_relevance: Computable proxy: replay quota grows with recent use and shrinks with familiarity. For an agent, count uses and novelty rather than judge importance.

source: Theta oscillations tag episodic memories for sleep-dependent consolidation (PLoS Biology 2026)
finding: EEG at learning decoded which word-object pairs would be kept over a nap versus wake. Learning-time theta (3-8 Hz) marked sleep-bound memories and predicted slow oscillation-spindle coupling, which predicted retention.
numbers: N=31 young adults, within-subject nap vs 2 h wake, 160 pairs learned. 16% +/- 4% of spindles coupled to a slow oscillation. Early theta power predicted later classifier accuracy at lags -0.96 to -0.05 s, peak r=0.39 at -0.45 s.
limits: Items are grouped by later retention, so the tag is inferred from outcomes and memory strength could drive it. Small N, one nap length, relevance not manipulated.
agent_relevance: First human neural evidence of a tag set at learning. Fits the design idea of deciding at write time, not at replay time.

source: Chen, Cheng (2026) Learning What to Remember: A Cognitively Grounded Multi-Factor Value Model for Agentic Memory (blind vs oracle retention)
finding: On LongMemEval-S, a goal-relevance score computed against the held-out question keeps 0.979 of gold evidence, but that peeks at the future query. With only the session topic, goal relevance falls to near chance.
numbers: 479 usable cases, keep 30%, 20 resampled splits. Blind: learned multi-factor value 0.770 +/- 0.011, uniform 0.657, self-relevance only 0.518, reliability only 0.497, recency 0.368, goal-only 0.286, emotion only 0.201, random 0.30. Oracle: learned 0.993, goal-only 0.979.
limits: One benchmark and a proxy objective (gold-evidence retention, not answer accuracy). API-free setting leaves several factors at 0. Weights learned on the same benchmark family.
agent_relevance: Direct test of keep by expected future use when the query is unknown at write time: recency and topic similarity fail, learned value wins. Any keep rule must be scored blind to the future query.

source: Chen, Cheng (2026) Learning What to Remember: A Cognitively Grounded Multi-Factor Value Model for Agentic Memory (gaps and learned weights)
finding: Learned blind weights put most mass on reliability and emotion, and none on goal relevance. Paired bootstrap gaps all exclude zero.
numbers: Weights: reliability 0.64, emotional intensity 0.55, self/user relevance 0.23, goal relevance 0.00. Gaps: +0.120 vs uniform (95% CI 0.091-0.149), +0.402 vs recency (0.350-0.452), +0.277 vs reliability-only (0.235-0.319).
limits: Weights reflect what LongMemEval gold looks like (user-stated, reliable facts) so may not transfer. An MLP ablation is reported to tie the linear value.
agent_relevance: The best predictor of later use was source reliability, not apparent relevance. Suggests tagging each lesson with where it came from (checked output vs model opinion).

source: Annapureddy, Thamatani (2026) The Epistemics of Agent Memory: Measuring, and Governing, the Consolidation Decision in Long-Horizon LLM Agents (Phase 2)
finding: A learned policy chooses per memory cluster to keep, summarise, extract a skill, distill a rule or forget, under a token budget. It raised task success but its forgetting was no better than chance.
numbers: +22.7% relative task success over best non-learned baseline (paired CI +1.89 to +11.34 pp), 7.17x compression. Forgetting precision 0.319 vs junk base rate 0.333. FORGET destroyed 74% of load-bearing clusters at least once; hard-config transfer regression -15.0 pp.
limits: Synthetic environment with a built-in oracle; the authors' pre-registered criterion was not fully met. Preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Strong caution: a learned forget rule can look good on success while deleting what later tasks need. Prefer demote-to-archive over delete.

source: Annapureddy, Thamatani (2026) ConsolidationBench leaderboard
finding: Production-style memory designs keep information but transfer nothing to new tasks. Only fixed-level and learned policies had any cross-level transfer.
numbers: Medium config, oracle ceiling success 0.632, transfer 0.333. Mem0-style: success 0.335, retention 0.531, transfer 0.000. SimpleMem-style 0.306, 0.485, 0.000. Fixed L2: 0.303, 0.480, transfer 0.233. Learned 0.368, 0.582, transfer 0.167. No-consolidation success 0.003. Eight of ten policies scored zero transfer.
limits: Benchmark built by the same authors; transfer axis defined by their oracle. A later check found Spearman -0.24 (n=12, CI -0.79 to +0.49) between a consolidation score and real transfer, so scores are weak proxies.
agent_relevance: Retention is not future usefulness. Our test of a keep rule should include use on a new problem, not recall of the old one.

source: Rana, Hung, Sun, Kunkel, Lawrence (2026) OBLIVION: Self-Adaptive Agentic Memory Control through Decay-Driven Activation
finding: Forgetting is cast as decay of accessibility, not deletion. Memories are strengthened when they help form a response. A hierarchy with all three layers beat fewer layers.
numbers: LongMemEval (S), GPT-4.1-mini: single layer 86.40%, L2+L3 (M4) 89.60%, full stack (M5) 90.60%. Token cost cut by 68% at 32K and 73% at 120K versus full context; at short spans it used about 5x (isolated) and 2x (2K) the tokens of full context. Latency 1.34x full context at 120K.
limits: Decay temperature is task and capacity dependent (T=50 behaves like always-on retrieval). Gains narrow at the longest span. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Closest AI match to strengthen-what-was-used: reinforcement from use, soft decay, nothing erased. Supports a use-count plus decay score for lessons.

source: Xie (2026) Learning to Forget: Sleep-Inspired Memory Consolidation for Resolving Proactive Interference in LLMs (SleepGate)
finding: A learned forgetting gate over the KV cache removes stale entries during periodic sleep cycles. On a toy proactive-interference test it kept retrieval high while five baselines stayed low.
numbers: 4-layer, 793K-parameter transformer. Accuracy 99.5% at interference depth 5 and 97.0% at depth 10. All five baselines (full KV, sliding window, H2O, StreamingLLM, decay-only) stayed under 18% at all depths.
limits: Toy model and synthetic benchmark, preliminary, single author. Not shown on a real LLM. Tests removal of superseded values, not relevance to future tasks.
agent_relevance: Evidence that removing superseded entries (not merely old ones) fixes interference. Relevant to dropping a lesson that a newer lesson replaces.

source: Shinde (2026) SCM: Sleep-Consolidated Memory with Algorithmic Forgetting for LLMs
finding: A research preview with importance tagging, NREM and REM-style offline consolidation and value-based forgetting. It reports perfect recall over ten-turn chats and 90.9% memory noise reduction.
numbers: Eight author-built tests; recall accuracy 100% over ten turns; noise reduced 90.9%; search under 1 ms with hundreds of concepts.
limits: Self-built tests, tiny scale, no comparison against real systems, no peer review. Weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Do not use as support. Listed so it is not mistaken for a validated result.

source: Yang et al (2026) SF-AMS: Strategic Forgetting for Structured Memory in LLM Agent
finding: A utility-driven survival score from usage, redundancy and time, with entity-level signals, beats LightMem, Mem0 and A-Mem on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-s. Removing the forgetting module hurts.
numbers: LoCoMo, Qwen2.5-7B F1: full model multi-hop 37.59 (+9.65 over best baseline), open-domain 32.76, temporal 29.24, single-hop 26.70. Without strategic forgetting: 16.11 single-hop, 18.78 multi-hop, 14.06 open-domain, 15.16 temporal. Without semantic salience: 21.70, 14.60, 10.60, 18.80. Without entity anchoring: 16.90, 13.50, 11.80, 16.20.
limits: The strategic-forgetting ablation removes the whole importance scoring, so it cannot separate forgetting from scoring. Authors' own ablation, one backbone. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A numbers-based case that a use-and-redundancy survival score helps. Test it against a keep-everything arm before copying.

source: Lin, Snell, Stoica, Gonzalez, Wang, Packer, Wooders (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: Pre-computing useful inferences about a context before the query arrives cuts test-time compute and lifts accuracy. The gain is larger when the query is easy to predict.
numbers: About 5x less test-time compute for the same accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME. Up to +13% (GSM-Symbolic) and +18% (AIME) accuracy with more sleep-time compute. Cost per query down 2.5x when shared across related queries.
limits: Modified benchmarks built for the method. It is offline anticipation, not selection of memories to drop. Query predictability drives the benefit.
agent_relevance: Matches the human finding: offline work pays only for expected future use. If we cannot predict the next task, skip the offline step.

source: Davidson, Pace-Schott (2021) review, discussion of power and replication
finding: The authors call the pattern a replication problem: labs run one participant per night, samples stay small, and winner's-curse inflation is likely. They urge larger N and multiverse analysis.
numbers: They cite Button et al on underpowered studies. The same paradigm often gives highly contrasting results between studies (Van Dongen 2012 vs a sleep-only repeat).
limits: Opinion of the review authors. The cell counts of the founding studies (about 17-25 per cell) fit the concern.
agent_relevance: Treat the relevance-gating effect as small and unstable. Our agent should test any relevance rule with enough runs to see a real gap.

source: Wilhelm 2011, Van Dongen 2012 and Wamsley 2016 compared on the wake condition (author synthesis from opened papers)
finding: The three studies disagree about what happens when people stay awake. Wilhelm: expectancy gave no gain in wake. Van Dongen: relevant items were forgotten more than irrelevant ones in wake. Wamsley: expectancy helped in wake as much as in sleep.
numbers: Wilhelm wake groups: informing subjects did not change retention (p>0.49). Van Dongen wake: relevant -5.0 vs irrelevant -3.3 (p=0.005). Wamsley: sleep x expectation interaction p between .33 and .99 across measures.
limits: Cross-study comparison is mine, not a formal test. Wake intervals and tasks differ (daytime 14 h vs about 7 to 8 h; word pairs vs picture locations vs maze).
agent_relevance: Three studies, three directions for wake: no effect, a cost, a gain. Do not rely on any one direction in agent design.

source: Theta tagging paper (2026): introduction statement on salience cues
finding: The introduction says salient cues (emotion, reward, future relevance) appear to be strengthened in the sleeping but not the waking brain, with 'though see' exceptions, and that animal work shows sleep replay grows with traversals and falls with familiarity.
numbers: Cites Huelin Gorriz 2023 for the animal result. No new counts.
limits: Literature framing, not data. Shows in a 2026 paper that the claim is still treated as open.
agent_relevance: Confirms that the tagging idea is current but, before this paper, lacked direct human evidence.
